title: DVARA: Frequency Gates for Adapting Frozen Underwater Image Enhancement Networks
content: Background. Deep underwater image enhancement (UIE) models are usually trained on a single data distribution and lose accuracy under unseen water conditions, while retraining the full network for every new condition is costly. Parameter-efficient adaptation of a frozen backbone is a cheaper alternative; the closest UIE work, UDAPA, adapts the input image rather than the network’s internal features. Methods. We propose DVARA, a frequency-gated adapter: a zero-initialized residual bottleneck module in which features are moved to the Fourier domain, split by a radial mask whose cutoff is a fixed fraction (0.25) of the spectrum at every resolution, re-weighted by per-channel learnable lowand high-frequency gates, and returned to the spatial domain. Inserting DVARA after each encoder and decoder block of a frozen FUnIE-GAN-based generator gives the adapted model PRAVAHA. Only the adapters are trained, on UIEB for 25 epochs with an L1 loss. We compare PRAVAHA against the frozen backbone, a plain spatial bottleneck adapter without the frequency split, and UDAPA, reporting PSNR on UIEB and, without further training, on EUVP and UFO-120. Results. PRAVAHA improved PSNR over the frozen backbone on all three test sets (UIEB 20.25 vs. 20.02 dB; EUVP 19.48 vs. 18.87 dB; UFO-120 19.53 vs. 19.09 dB). Relative to UDAPA it was higher on UIEB (+0.06 dB) and EUVP (+0.10 dB) and lower on UFO-120 (−0.17 dB); averaged over the three sets, both methods gained 0.43 dB over the backbone. The plain adapter fell below the frozen backbone on every test set. No repeated runs or significance tests are reported. Conclusions. Frequency-gated internal adaptation of a frozen UIE backbone with DVARA gives modest gains comparable to input-side alignment, with each approach ahead on different benchmarks. Repeated runs, additional metrics and additional backbones are needed to establish whether these differences are reliable.
